data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The smallest positive integer is 18, derived from a quotient-rounding observation: 18 is the unique integer in [0, 35) for which floor(x/5) and floor(x/7) differ by exactly 2, reflecting that the remainders 3 and 4 differ by the same gap as the divisors' offsets from 10.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the 'quotient-remainder balance' is not a valid invariant, this is an invalid fabrication","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If another x < 18 satisfies quotient_diff = remainder_diff = 1, minimality fails","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the balance condition is not sufficient for the congruences, the derivation is incomplete","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"For x = 18: floor(18/5) = 3 and floor(18/7) = 2, differing by 1 (not 2 \u2014 disanalogy). But consider remainders: 18 = 3\u00b75 + 3 and 18 = 2\u00b77 + 4. The quotients (3 and 2) and remainders (3 and 4) are related: quotient_5 \u2212 quotient_7 = 1 and remainder_7 \u2212 remainder_5 = 1. This 'quotient-remainder balance' (where the difference in quotients compensates the difference in remainders) characterizes the solution. For x < 18, no such balance exists: x = 13 gives quotients 2, 1 (diff 1) but remainders 3, 6 (diff 3); x = 8 gives 1, 1 and 3, 1. Only x = 18 has quotient_diff = remainder_diff = 1. So 18 is minimal.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
